newsitem.title: India: Kashmir leader sworn in, separatists vow to fight on.
newsitem.headline: Kashmir leader sworn in, separatists vow to fight on.

text.p: Kashmir's new chief minister tearfully took office in an emotional ceremony on Monday as separatists in the troubled region vowed to continue their fight against his government.

Under tight security, National Conference chairman Farooq Abdullah was sworn in as chief minister of Jammu and Kashmir state in a ceremony in Srinagar, the state's summer capital and the focus of a separatist revolt that began in 1990.
"We must turn trouble-torn Kashmir again into heaven," Abdullah, 59, said in a speech after the ceremony, during which he twice broke down in tears.
"For that I appeal to the people of India and Kashmir for their support. I warn Pakistan not to stick its leg into our business," he said, speaking in Urdu.
India accuses Pakistan of arming separatist guerrillas in the region who seek independence or union with Pakistan. Pakistan says it only provides moral and diplomatic support.
Schools, shops and businesses were closed after separatist political parties which reject Abdullah's government called for a strike throughout the Himalayan region on Wednesday.

"The so-called legislative assembly and the regime led by Dr Farooq Abdullah, an extension and instrumentality of Indian neo-imperialism, is neither acceptable to the people of Jammu and Kashmir nor has it any credence," said Gulam Nabi Sumji, a spokesman for the All-Parties Hurriyat (Freedom) Conference.
Hurriyat, a leading coalition of about 30 political groups, boycotted the polls which it described as a "mockery of Kashmiri aspirations".
Sumji called for a tripartite dialogue among New Delhi, Islamabad and the state's people to permanently resolve the dispute.
Abdullah, dressed in a Nehru jacket and peaked lambs'-wool cap, smiled and hugged many of the guests at the oath-taking ceremony in a large conference hall on picturesque Dal Lake.
"The last drop of my blood will go to defend India," Abdullah said later, speaking through tears. "Kashmir has been, is, and always will be, part of India."

Senior Indian politicians from a range of parties attended the ceremony, closing ranks with Abdullah despite political differences to present a united face for the state, the only Moslem majority province in predominantly Hindu India.
Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's government and its allies said they would back Abdullah's bid to win autonomy for Kashmir.

"Today marks the fulfilment of Prime Minister Deve Gowda's promise to restore to Kashmir its status as paradise by starting the democratic process," said Indian Information and Broadcasting Minister C.M. Ibrahim.

Former prime minister V.P. Singh told Abdullah: "Your tears symbolise a moment in Kashmir's troubled history when we begin to wipe away the tears of those mothers who lost so many of their children in the violence."
Abdullah contested the polls on a promise of autonomy for the region, which includes Hindu-dominated Jammu, the predominantly Moslem Kashmir valley, and Buddhist Ladakh.
Two dozen ministers were sworn in with Abdullah.
Last week his party won 58 seats -- an absolute majority -- in the 87-member assembly in the first state polls since 1987.
Kashmiri analysts said Abdullah must first reconcile the separatists and try to put the battered economy back on track.
Police and hospital sources say more than 20,000 people have been killed in insurgency-related violence since 1990.
